description: The hand-verified expected result for the negative Gitleaks fixture that carries one record whose StartLine is present but is not an integer -- the numeric-looking string "5". Every value was derived by reading the fixture and the authored contracts in harness/lib/normalize/, never by running the adapter and recording what it printed. Where this file and harness/lib/normalize/adapters/gitleaks.py disagree, the disagreement is the finding: diagnose it rather than overwriting this file to match. Key names follow expected/reject-sarif-unresolvable-path.rows.json, the first negative expected file in this folder and the template for the rest, and the two gitleaks siblings that extend it, so one generic loader reads them all; the additive structure is start_line_policy, which is this fixture's subject, and boundary_case, which is this fixture's Gitleaks-specific twist. Two things a reader must take from this paragraph before anything else. First, the fixture carries TWO companion records with no start_line, by two different routes -- /2 has the key deleted and /3 carries an explicit null -- and both are rows with start_line null rather than rejections; a reader expecting one companion will count wrong. Second, the defective record's value sits at its file's real last line: that file is five lines long and the value is the string "5". The type is the fault and the line is not a fault at all, the two are independent, and boundary_case keeps them apart.
scanner_class_note: Fixed per tool by AAP 0.5.4's class table and authored as a constant in the adapter (SCANNER_CLASS). Trivy is the single tool whose class varies per record; this one never does, so no row below takes its class from record content, and the rejected record changes the class of nothing.
rules: No user-specified rule governs this file. review_rules returns exactly one line, 'No user rules provided.', which is the whole document; AAP 0.7 says the same. No rule is cited or invented here, and the absence is not licence to lower the bar. The bar on this file is three things at once: a rejection class asserted against the module that defines it rather than against the fixture's file name, a security property stated under redaction_invariant and asserted against this file's own bytes, and a derivation a reader can re-perform from the fixture without running anything.

fixture.record_keys: 18 on five of the six elements -- the full key set the pinned Gitleaks emits -- and 17 on /2, whose StartLine key the derivation deleted. That single difference is the point of /2 and is not a defect in the fixture.
fixture.record_key_order_note: Every element's keys are in the order harness/artifacts/raw/gitleaks.json's own record carries them, and /2's seventeen are that same order with StartLine removed -- checked by comparing key lists rather than by eye, so a reader can re-derive the derivation as a deletion rather than a rewrite.
fixture.derivation: A negative fixture is derived from the captured one rather than being an excerpt of it, so the provenance is stated as a derivation -- except for /0, which is captured output carried verbatim. /0 is byte-equal to the raw artifact's sole element and to the positive fixture's element 0. /1 and /5 are byte-equal to the positive fixture's elements 1 and 5, reused unchanged so that two of this fixture's rows are rows that file already fixes. /2 is the positive fixture's element 2 with its StartLine key deleted outright, leaving seventeen keys. /3 is the positive fixture's element 3 with its StartLine value replaced by an explicit JSON null, leaving eighteen. /4 is the defective record: the positive fixture's element 4, relocated to its file's last line and given that line as a string -- StartLine "5" where the captured record carried the integer 3, with EndLine, both columns and the line component of the fingerprint moved with it so that the record stays internally consistent.
fixture.defective_element_derivation_check: Five of /4's eighteen keys differ from the positive fixture's element 4 -- StartLine, EndLine, StartColumn, EndColumn and the trailing fingerprint -- and the other thirteen are byte-identical, in the raw record's key order. Four of those five are the relocation and carry no fault: an integer EndLine, two integer columns and a consistent fingerprint. Exactly one is the fault: StartLine's JSON type. That is what makes the rejection attributable to the type alone, and it is why the relocation is described here rather than left for a reader to notice.
fixture.why_the_relocation_and_not_a_bare_retype: Retyping 3 to "3" would have tested the same branch. Moving the value to 5 buys a second property for nothing: 5 is that file's real last line, so the fixture also proves the adapter does not reject a value for being out of range when what is wrong with it is its type, and does not accept one for being in range when its type is wrong. boundary_case states the consequence in full.
fixture.captured_provenance: Established by comparing each element key by key and in key order against every element of the positive fixture and against the raw artifact's single element, not by eye. /0 matches the raw element exactly, which is what makes it captured rather than derived; /1 and /5 match positive-fixture elements exactly; /2, /3 and /4 match nothing, which is what makes them demonstrably this fixture's own derivations rather than something the tool emitted. The recorded sha256 above is what makes a later edit to the fixture visible: these values are re-derived when the fixture changes, never adjusted to keep a test green.
fixture.not_records: There is nothing in this artifact that is not a record. The top level is an array of six objects and every one of them is a finding record; the count unit is the element, so no reading of this document can arrive at any number other than six.

routing.detected_by: normalize.shape.is_sarif returns false -- a SARIF artifact is a version of '2.1.0' together with a runs array, and those two together are the whole test. A bare array carries neither, and cannot: a JSON array has no string keys to look either of them up under.
routing.routing_decision: normalize.shape.route('gitleaks', doc) returns tool 'gitleaks', shape 'native', adapter 'gitleaks', scanner_class 'secret'
routing.not_a_shape_failure: No normalize.shape.UnknownArtifactShape is expected here, and a test asserting one against this fixture would be asserting the wrong thing. The enclosing document is a well-formed Gitleaks artifact and routes cleanly; exactly one record inside it is defective, and the adapter rejects that record while still emitting the other five. The fixtures that own shape-detection failure are near-sarif-version-only.json, near-sarif-runs-only.json and unknown-shape.json.
routing.the_document_level_fault_this_fixture_is: adapters/gitleaks.py raises GitleaksAdapterError rather than rejecting where the top level is not an array, because reconcile.count_records counts zero records in a non-array document and a rejection would then make rows plus rejections exceed the record count. That behaviour belongs to a call-level assertion, not to this fixture, whose top level is an array.
routing.negative_routing_test: The mandated negative routing assertion -- that a native artifact must not route to the SARIF adapter -- belongs to test_shape_routing_negative.py. This file fixes only what the gitleaks adapter produces.

field_order_authority: harness/lib/normalize/emit.py, the FIELDS constant -- the only place the order is written down and the iteration order of every writer, reader and comparison. Every row below carries all twelve keys in that order, present-with-null rather than omitted, which is what keeps the CSV column set uniform. The adapter's own FIELDS is an authored copy that must agree with it by construction, because AAP 0.6.4 permits an adapter to import paths and severity and nothing else.
absence_convention: Absence is JSON null here and in findings.json, and an empty field in findings.csv. tool, scanner_class, rule_id, message, severity_norm, path and in_scope are never absent -- exactly emit.REQUIRED_FIELDS. start_line's presence in the permitted set is this fixture's whole subject: it is why an absent start_line is a row and not a rejection, and why a present-but-wrong one cannot be emitted as null.

allowlist.note: in_scope is decided by that file alone. The globs are not copied here: the allowlist is the single authority and stays byte-exact. The glob each row matched is recorded per row under row_derivations, and the one row matching none of them is named there too.

reference_behaviours.behaviour: a start_line present but not an integer, rejected under its own class with no coercion
reference_behaviours.what_this_file_fixes: One rejection under non_integer_start_line for the string "5", with the sub-reason retained, alongside the five rows the same artifact still produces. Neither 5 nor null is written for that record anywhere.
reference_behaviours.why_it_belongs_here: A numeric-looking string is the one wrong value an implementation is most likely to accept: int("5") succeeds, so a coercing adapter produces a plausible row and a passing test. Fixing the rejection here is what makes coercion detectable.

reference_behaviours.behaviour: the permitted absent start_line, by both of its routes, and the start_line_absent counter
reference_behaviours.what_this_file_fixes: Two rows with start_line null -- one from a deleted key, one from an explicit null -- and start_line_absent at 2. reject-gitleaks-unresolvable-path.rows.json lists exactly this behaviour as one it does not exercise, so this file is where it is fixed.
reference_behaviours.why_it_belongs_here: An implementation that tests isinstance(value, int) against a plain dict lookup, with no distinction between an absent key and a wrongly-typed value, rejects both of these rows while producing the correct rejection count for the wrong reason. missing_key_hazard states the blast radius.

reference_behaviours.behaviour: a rejection detail that names a value's type rather than rendering the value
reference_behaviours.what_this_file_fixes: The expected detail is 'StartLine is a str rather than an integer'. The offending value appears in this document as evidence of what the artifact contained, and in the detail not at all.
reference_behaviours.why_it_belongs_here: AAP 0.5.4 requires the parser reason retained verbatim, and the adapter's _safe_value_repr renders only None, a bool, an int and a float and otherwise names the type -- so the verbatim channel cannot become a leak channel. A str is deliberately in the second group, and this fixture's offending value is a str, which is what exercises it.

resolution_context.path_base_source: harness/artifacts/logs/runner-metadata.json, tools.gitleaks.path_base -- read as input, never assumed. Its record_path_field is 'File', which is the field resolve_gitleaks_path reads; the adapter's own _FILE_KEY is only the default that function falls back to.
resolution_context.path_base_value_note: The recorded base is the pinned scan root. Its absolute form is deliberately not reproduced here: no absolute path appears anywhere in this file, and these rows hold for whatever absolute root the adapter is given.
resolution_context.recorded_invocation_shape: Eighteen invocations, each handed exactly one root-relative directory, with the runner's working directory set to the scan root.
resolution_context.invocation_source: runner-metadata.json tools.gitleaks.invocation_form and working_directory -- invocations_per_run 18, target_passing_style 'exactly one root-relative path per invocation, one invocation per scope directory', working directory equal to the scan root -- corroborated independently by harness/bin/run-gitleaks.sh, which cds to the scan root and then loops one directory per invocation.
resolution_context.why_the_base_is_invocation_dependent: gitleaks dir takes exactly one path and reports relative to the process working directory when handed more, so the base is a property of the invocation rather than of the tool (AAP 0.5.4). Both shapes are real: the historical harness AAP 0.2.3 describes passed all eighteen scope directories to a single invocation, and this provisioning passes one per invocation.
resolution_context.invariance_across_the_two_shapes: Here the two shapes give the same base, because the runner's working directory is the scan root, so every path below holds under either reading. That is a fact about this provisioning rather than a licence to skip reading the metadata -- a runner that cds elsewhere would need these paths re-derived, and no runner may be edited to make one shape true (AAP 0.3.2).
resolution_context.path_basis_authority: harness/lib/normalize/paths.py, BASIS_ALREADY_ROOT_RELATIVE -- the basis resolve_recorded_path records where the recorded base and the scan root are the same location, so the reported File was already root-relative and the join changed nothing. The basis says so rather than implying a resolution that did no work.
resolution_context.path_kind_authority: harness/lib/normalize/paths.py, path_kind_for: no '!' separator and no leading '..' segment, so every emitted path names a location inside the scanned tree. Whether the file exists on disk is a separate question paths.py never asks -- nothing in it stats the filesystem -- and each of the five surviving paths was checked against the pinned tree separately, per row.
resolution_context.severity_source: None. The eighteen keys a pinned-Gitleaks record carries include no severity-like field, and no element of this fixture carries one, so every emitted row goes through severity.SeverityResult.absent().
resolution_context.severity_basis_authority: harness/lib/normalize/severity.py, BASIS_NO_VOCABULARY. absent() carries severity_native null, severity_norm Info and that basis, and its __post_init__ refuses a severity_native on it -- so the absence is structural rather than a convention a caller has to remember. Info is not hard-coded in the adapter.
resolution_context.severity_selected_entry_note: null on this path: nothing was used to derive the band, so there is neither a label nor a score entry to record. The band comes from a policy fixed before any output was observed, and no native literal is synthesised -- inventing one would put a literal into oss-scan-results/severity-map.md that the tool never emitted.
resolution_context.severity_map_consequence: The tally is fed once per emitted row and never for a rejected record, so severity-map.md can name gitleaks as a tool that defines no severity vocabulary with a row count behind the statement, and that count is five here rather than six. A rejected record contributing a tally entry would report an entry against a row the dataset does not contain.
resolution_context.package_coordinate: null on every row. A secret finding names a code location rather than a package, and this shape supplies no coordinate to carry. AAP 0.5.4's unformable-coordinate rejection reaches dependency-oriented records only, so the absence here is not a rejection condition -- not on the row whose path is a lockfile, and not on the rejected record whose path is a manifest.
resolution_context.cwe_and_cve: null on every row. The shape carries no weakness or advisory identifier; deriving a CWE from a rule id would be inference of exactly the kind AAP 0.5.4 forbids.

start_line_policy.statement: This fixture's whole subject is the difference between a start_line that is ABSENT and a start_line that is PRESENT and of the wrong type. Absence is permitted: start_line is one of the five fields AAP 0.8.2 allows to be absent, so a record that states no line yields a row with start_line null. A start_line present but not an integer is a rejection: the producer asserted a line number and supplied something that is not one, and there is no reading of that which is not a guess.
start_line_policy.no_coercion: "5" must not become 5, in any file this pipeline writes. Coercing it would invent data -- it would assert that the producer stated an integer when what the producer stated was a string -- and AAP 0.5.4 is explicit that a record which cannot be attributed with certainty is rejected and counted, never inferred into a field. No coercion is recorded as expected behaviour anywhere in this file, for the rejected record or for any row. The adapter's own comment gives the second reason: int() accepts more than a faithful round trip should, so int("1_2") is 12 and a coercing implementation would silently agree with an artifact that said something else.
start_line_policy.why_a_rejection_rather_than_a_row_with_n: Emitting the record with start_line null would record an absence the producer did not state, and would make a defective record indistinguishable from the two legitimate absences sitting beside it in this very fixture -- which is the sharpest reason available and is why those two are in the fixture at all. Emitting it with 5 would be worse: it would put a number in the dataset that no field of that record contains as a number in that position. Counting it under a named class is the only outcome that neither drops the record nor invents a value for it.
start_line_policy.adapter_contract: harness/lib/normalize/adapters/gitleaks.py, _start_line. Four outcomes, and only two of them reject: StartLine absent from the record -> (None, no rejection); StartLine present as an explicit null -> (None, no rejection), the same first branch, since the lookup yields None either way; StartLine present as a bool, or present and not an int -> non_integer_start_line, with the bool test ordered first; StartLine an int below 1 -> non_integer_start_line with a different detail, since gitleaks numbers lines from one.
start_line_policy.explicit_null_is_absence_not_a_type_faul: The one judgement in this policy a reader might expect to go the other way, so it is stated rather than left to the code. JSON null is exactly what emit.py writes for an absent optional field, so a producer's null is the producer saying nothing rather than saying something wrong. Reading it as 'present but not an integer' would reject a legal record, and it would make findings.json internally inconsistent: the same null that means absence when this pipeline writes it would mean a defect when it reads it. record.get() collapses the two onto one branch, which is the behaviour rather than an accident of the lookup.
start_line_policy.classification_position: step 5 of the adapter's fixed five-step order -- shape, rule identifier, message, path, start_line. It is last, so a record defective in both its path and its start_line is classified by its path. The defective record here has a perfectly resolvable path, which is what lets it reach step 5 at all, and its path is deliberately not recorded in this file.

cases_present_in_this_fixture.case: start_line present as an integer well inside a long file
start_line present as an integer inside a short file
the StartLine key deleted from the record altogether
StartLine present as an explicit JSON null
start_line present as the numeric-looking string "5", at the value of its file's real last line
cases_present_in_this_fixture.expected: a counted rejection under non_integer_start_line, no row, no coercion

cases_present_in_this_fixture.case: start_line present as an integer, on a path outside the twelve globs
cases_present_in_this_fixture.expected: a row with start_line 17 and in_scope false

start_line_policy.two_absence_routes_not_one: Worth stating plainly, because a reader expecting a single companion row will count wrong. This fixture carries TWO records with no start_line and they reach the same early return by two different routes: /2's StartLine key is absent, so record.get returns None because the key is missing, and /3's StartLine is an explicit null, so record.get returns None because that is the value. Both are rows with start_line null; neither is a rejection; both increment start_line_absent. Covering both is deliberate -- an implementation could guard the missing key and still reject the explicit null, or use a sentinel default that distinguishes them and then treat the null as a wrongly-typed value.

missing_key_hazard.statement: The load-bearing reason the companion rows exist. An implementation that tests isinstance(value, int) against the result of a plain dict lookup -- with no distinction between a key that is absent and a key whose value is of the wrong type -- rejects both. That single conflation would reject two of this fixture's five rows, and it does not stop there.
blast_radius: Every Trivy vulnerability record. harness/lib/normalize/adapters/trivy.py records that line information appears on secrets and misconfigurations rather than on vulnerabilities, which is Trivy 0.74.0's own report shape (AAP 0.5.4: start_line is section-dependent). A missing-key rejection would discard that artifact's entire vulnerability section under a class describing a defect none of those records has.

The whole Dependency-Check artifact. harness/lib/normalize/adapters/dependency_check.py holds start_line at a module-level constant of None for every row, because that tool reports at dependency granularity and carries no line information at all. Under a missing-key rejection its row count would be zero and its rejection count would be its record count.

Every Gitleaks finding a future artifact reports without a line. This shape's own exposure: the eighteen-key record always carries StartLine today, so the hazard is invisible in this run's own artifact and is only testable through a derived fixture -- which is what /2 and /3 are.
missing_key_hazard.measured_in_this_run: Stated as a structural hazard rather than an observed one, because this run's own Gitleaks artifact could not have exposed it: it holds a single element and that element carries an integer StartLine. The hazard would bite the moment a producer omitted one, which is exactly why it is tested here rather than left to be discovered then.
missing_key_hazard.what_the_test_must_assert: Not merely that the rejection count is 1. It must assert that the two absent-start_line records are present as rows, each with start_line null, because a conflating implementation produces the correct rejection count for the wrong reason -- three rejections and three rows would fail, but so would any assertion that only counted rejections.

boolean_hazard.statement: isinstance(True, int) is True in Python: bool is a subclass of int, so an unguarded integer check admits True as line 1 and False as line 0. gitleaks._start_line guards it explicitly and the guard is ordered first -- isinstance(raw, bool) is tested before not isinstance(raw, int) -- so a boolean is classified as non_integer_start_line rather than emitted. The detail would name it in full, since _safe_value_repr renders a bool rather than naming its type.
boolean_hazard.why_absent_here: The only StartLine values this fixture contains are the integers 3090, 241 and 17, the string "5", one deleted key and one explicit null. The prompt for this file allows for a boolean case and this fixture does not carry one, so no expected rejection is recorded for it: an expectation for a record that is not in the fixture would be an assertion nothing can run.
boolean_hazard.not_covered_by_a_sibling_either: Checked against the fixtures themselves, so the gap is stated rather than assumed covered: none of the four sibling non-integer fixtures carries a boolean either -- reject-sarif-non-integer-start-line.sarif uses the string "72", reject-checkov-non-integer-start-line.json the string "20", reject-joern-non-integer-start-line.json the string "417" and reject-trivy-non-integer-start-line.json the string "62".
boolean_hazard.cover_with: a derived fixture carrying StartLine true, asserted to reject under non_integer_start_line with a detail naming the boolean rather than an integer

below_one_hazard.statement: An integer below 1 is rejected under the same class with a different detail, because gitleaks numbers lines from one: 0 is not a line and a negative value is not one either -- emit.py would refuse a negative outright, and emitting 0 would assert a line that does not exist. Naming it here keeps the class's three routes legible: wrong type, boolean, and out of range.
below_one_hazard.cover_with: a derived fixture carrying StartLine 0, and one carrying -1

start_line_policy.the_class_covers_three_routes_so_the_det: paths.REJECT_CLASSES is a closed set, so all three routes share one class name and the detail carries the sub-reason -- exactly as AAP 0.5.4 does for the uriBaseId terminal cases. A test asserting only the class would pass against a boolean or a zero as readily as against this fixture's string, which is why the expected detail is recorded verbatim under rejections.

boundary_case.statement: The Gitleaks-specific twist, and the one thing in this fixture most likely to be misread as a second fault. The defective record names core/src/main/resources/org/apache/spark/ui/static/package.json, which is exactly five lines and eighty bytes at the pin, and its StartLine is the string "5". So the value is type-invalid while sitting at the file's real last line: in range and wrongly typed at once.
boundary_case.the_two_faults_are_independent: There is one fault, not two. The type is wrong; the line is not. Had the record carried the integer 5 it would have been a row, because 5 is a line that file has -- and had it carried the string "9000" it would have been the same rejection, because the class is decided before any range question is asked. This file must not conflate them, and does not: the rejection's expected detail names the type and says nothing about range, and no out-of-range expectation is recorded for this record.

file_at_the_pin.content_shape: an object carrying a name, a license and a module type -- no dependencies block, and no lockfile beside it
file_at_the_pin.why_it_matters: It is the only manifest-shaped file inside the twelve authoritative globs (AAP 0.2.1), which is why nothing in scope resolves to a package and why OSV-Scanner writes no artifact at all. It appears across several fixtures for that reason, which makes it the file whose line bounds are easiest to get wrong.

boundary_case.no_row_for_this_file_exists_in_this_expe: Stated explicitly rather than left to be inferred from the rows. This fixture's only element naming that file is the defective one, and a rejected record contributes no row, so the constraint that no start_line for that file may exceed 5 holds here vacuously -- there is no such start_line to bound. A reader checking that constraint programmatically will find zero rows to check, and that is the correct result rather than a gap.
boundary_case.where_a_row_for_it_does_exist: expected/gitleaks.rows.json's counterpart row for the same file carries the integer 3, which is inside the file's five lines. This fixture's derivation moved that coordinate to the last line and changed its type; the positive sibling is where the sound row for the file is fixed.

verified_line_counts_at_the_pin.note: Measured in the pinned tree at 59b8a4489c878fa3a9aa6b7fbae760f2fc80eb9d, which is the tree the artifact describes. Two of these differ at the branch tip and are recorded per row where they do; the pin governs. Every start_line emitted below is an integer at or below its own file's count.

rejection_boundary.statement: A start_line present but not an integer is a rejection. An absent start_line is a kept row with start_line null. Those are the two sides of this fixture's boundary, and it carries records on both -- three sound integers, two absences and one wrongly-typed value.
rejection_boundary.why_it_can_only_be_a_rejection: start_line is one of the five fields absence is permitted for, so unlike an unresolvable path there IS a valid row shape available -- which is precisely why the distinction has to be drawn on the producer's assertion rather than on the schema's tolerance. The producer supplied a value; that value is not a line number; emitting the row with null would misreport the artifact as silent, and emitting it with a coerced integer would misreport the artifact as having stated a number. AAP 0.5.4 settles it: reject rather than infer, count the rejection under its class, and keep the record visible.

not_a_rejection.case: start_line absent altogether, by either route
not_a_rejection.expected: a kept row with start_line null, counted under start_line_absent
not_a_rejection.evidence: Absence is permitted for start_line by AAP 0.8.2 and emit.OPTIONAL_FIELDS carries it, so the row is valid and complete.
not_a_rejection.where: /2 and /3, which become rows[2] and rows[3]

not_a_rejection.case: a path resolving outside the twelve authoritative globs
not_a_rejection.expected: a kept row with in_scope false, counted under rows_out_of_scope
not_a_rejection.evidence: Out of scope means kept and marked, never rejected (AAP 0.9.3). The real out-of-glob files in the pinned tree include dev/package-lock.json, ui-test/package-lock.json and docs/Gemfile.lock.
not_a_rejection.where: /5, which becomes rows[4] with in_scope false

not_a_rejection.case: an in-range integer line in a five-line file
not_a_rejection.expected: a kept row with that integer
not_a_rejection.evidence: Range is not a fault this class covers below 1, and above 1 it is not checked at all: nothing in the adapter compares a line against a file's length, and nothing in paths.py stats the filesystem. The bounds recorded per row here are this document's own verification of the fixture, not a behaviour of the pipeline.
not_a_rejection.where: the one candidate is the rejected record, whose value is a string; expected/gitleaks.rows.json fixes the sound case for the same file

not_a_rejection.case: an archive member or a location above the root
not_a_rejection.expected: a kept row with in_scope false, counted in non_filesystem_paths
not_a_rejection.evidence: Serialized as <container-relative-to-root>!<member> with '!' the single separator, and with ../ segments preserved rather than normalized. No File value in this fixture takes that route.

rejection_boundary.no_guessed_start_line: The rejected record is rejected and counted, never given a start_line. Nothing in this file supplies a line number for it -- not 5, not null-as-though-absent, and not the integer EndLine that sits beside the defective StartLine in the same record. That EndLine is deliberately left unread: reading it would be inferring the start from the end, and it is the most tempting inference in this fixture precisely because it is an integer of the same value.
rejection_boundary.no_guessed_path: Nor is the rejected record given a path, a severity or a row of any kind. It resolved a path successfully on its way to step 5, and that resolved path appears in no field of this document, because a record that produced no row contributes no field to the dataset. Its file is named in prose under boundary_case, which is a statement about the fixture rather than a value asserted for the record.
rejection_boundary.endline_is_unread_on_the_companion_rows_: /2 and /3 each carry an integer EndLine while their start_line is null, so the same inference is available on a row and is likewise not taken. A companion row whose start_line had been filled from EndLine would look correct and would be asserting a line the producer never put in that field.

counts.raw_count_unit: one element of the top-level array -- the unit normalize.reconcile.count_records walks independently of row construction; its _count_gitleaks is the array's length and nothing else
counts.raw_count_authority: harness/lib/normalize/reconcile.py, count_records('gitleaks', doc), doc), which builds no row, resolves no path and maps no severity. It is the independent half of the identity: a count taken from the traversal that builds the rows would satisfy the assertion while testing nothing. For this shape it also means the count is unaffected by any record's content -- a defective element counts exactly like a sound one, which is what makes the arithmetic below a real check.
counts.rejections_by_class_note: One class, one record, and the class is the one the fixture's name states. Unlike reject-gitleaks-unresolvable-path.rows.json there is no divergence to explain here: paths.REJECT_NON_INTEGER_START_LINE is raised by the adapter's own step 5 rather than returned from a resolver, so the fixture name and the class coincide.
counts.every_element_yields_exactly_one_outcome: One row or one rejection per element, never both and never neither -- _adapt_record returns a single value of one of the two types, so the property is structural rather than asserted. Five elements carry a non-empty RuleID and Description, a non-empty File and a StartLine that is either an integer of at least 1 or absent, and become rows; the sixth carries a string where a line belongs and is counted.
counts.parse_status_authority: harness/lib/normalize/cli.py, PARSE_STATUS_PARTIAL = 'partial', assigned as partial where there are rejections and clean where there are none. Partial is right precisely because the adapter did not abandon the artifact: every parsable record was emitted and the one rejected record is counted under its class, with its parser reason retained. This is deliberately not normalize.reconcile's STATUS_PASS / STATUS_FAIL / STATUS_NOT_APPLICABLE vocabulary, which describes an assertion's outcome rather than an artifact's parse.
counts.row_order: fixture order, preserved, with the rejected element contributing nothing to it -- so rows[4] comes from element /5. Both output files use this order and emit.py compares them ordered row by row, so an expected file in any other order would assert something the pipeline does not promise.
counts.defect_position_is_deliberate: The defective element sits at /4, second from last rather than at either end, so an adapter that stopped on the first defect would emit four rows and one that dropped the tail after it would emit four as well. Either is visible against the five above, and the surviving element after it is the out-of-glob row, which is the one a careless implementation is likeliest to drop for a second reason.

counters_authority: harness/lib/normalize/adapters/gitleaks.py, COUNTER_KEYS as returned by new_counters(): six authored keys, then one path_kind_* per normalize.paths.PATH_KINDS member and one severity_basis_* per normalize.severity.BASIS_VALUES member -- fifteen keys in that order, which is the key set and the order above. Deliberately absent from it, and so from here: any adapter-side count of records walked, rows or rejections. Those are len(rows), len(rejections) and reconcile.count_records, and a plausible substitute published here is how the independent-traversal requirement would quietly be lost.
counters_note: Three numbers a reader must not 'correct'. First, start_line_absent is 2, not 1: the two absent-start_line records are two rows and each increments it -- see start_line_policy.two_absence_routes_not_one. Second, severity_absent, severity_basis_no_vocabulary and path_kind_tree_file are 5 rather than 6, and rows_in_scope plus rows_out_of_scope is 4 + 1 = 5: all four are incremented after step 5, so the record rejected at step 5 contributes to none of them even though its path resolved cleanly on the way there. That asymmetry is the classification order made visible, not a miscount. Third, multi_location_records is the one counter a rejected record could still have moved, since the adapter takes it before the path step; it is 0 here because SymlinkFile is the empty string on all six elements, including /4.

counters_aap_0_5_4_reported.note: The four counters AAP 0.5.4 has reported per tool. Two of them -- multi_location_records and non_filesystem_paths -- are keys of this adapter's own counter set and appear above with the same values. The other two are not: a Gitleaks record carries no CWE or CVE field at all, so no record can be multi-valued in either, and the adapter keys no counter it could never increment. They are stated here as 0 by construction so the four required numbers are all present in one place, and so that the difference between 'measured 0' and '0 because the field does not exist in this shape' is legible rather than inferred from a missing key.

redaction_invariant.requirement: AAP 0.5.4: Gitleaks runs with redaction so a matched secret's value never enters an artifact, and no adapter carries a secret value into any field. This file is committed to git -- .gitignore line 31 matches artifacts/ and nothing under oss-scan-results/ -- so the invariant has to hold of this file as written, not only of the dataset the adapter produces. A negative expected file carries one exposure a positive one does not: a rejection detail, which AAP 0.5.4 requires retained verbatim and which is therefore quoted here in full.
redaction_invariant.message_source_on_every_row: Description, the rule's own description. Never Secret, never Match, and never Message, which is a git commit message rather than a description. There is deliberately no fallback: every candidate would either infer content the tool did not state or carry a captured value into the field.
redaction_invariant.keys_never_read_authority: harness/lib/normalize/adapters/gitleaks.py, NEVER_READ_FIELDS. Fingerprint is excluded even though this artifact's values are composites of a path, a rule and a line: in commit mode it also carries a commit identity, and a field whose safety depends on which mode ran is not a field to read. EndLine's presence in this list is load-bearing for this fixture in particular -- three of its elements make reading it look attractive.
redaction_invariant.keys_read_authority: harness/lib/normalize/adapters/gitleaks.py, SOURCE_FIELDS -- the four keys a row is built from, named one at a time. The record is never copied, spread or iterated into a row, which is what makes the invariant structural there; here it is upheld by deriving each of the twelve values from those four keys and fixed constants alone.
redaction_invariant.rejection_detail_safety: The rejected record's detail is quoted verbatim below and contains no value from the record: the adapter composes it from the key's name, the value's type name and fixed prose. _safe_value_repr renders only None, a bool, an int and a float and otherwise names a value's type, and a str is deliberately in the second group -- 'ordinarily safe' is not the standard this invariant is held to. This fixture's offending value is a str, so it is the case that exercises the choice, and it is why the detail says a type where the SARIF sibling's says a value.
redaction_invariant.record_identity_safety: The rejection's record_identity carries the array index and the rule identifier and nothing else, because that is what the adapter passes into make_rejection at step 5. Both are identifying fields rather than captured values. Note what is absent by comparison with a path rejection: no reported_path and no File, since the resolver did not build this rejection.
redaction_invariant.symlink_file_is_the_one_exception: SymlinkFile is the single key outside SOURCE_FIELDS the adapter looks at, and only through a predicate returning a bool. It is a filesystem path rather than a captured value, it is never emitted, and it is never substituted for an absent File. It is empty on all six elements here, so it decides nothing beyond leaving multi_location_records at 0.
redaction_invariant.check_performed: Every distinct Match, Secret and Fingerprint value in the fixture -- eight values across the six elements -- was tested as a substring against the whole of this file. Zero hits, which is the required result. The check covers prose as well as row fields, and three drafting consequences follow from it: no sentence here quotes the placeholder string the runner's redaction flag substitutes for a captured value, nowhere is a path, a rule id and a line number joined into one colon-separated string, since that is the shape of this artifact's fingerprint values, and no expression quoted from a scanned source file is reproduced.
redaction_invariant.upstream_protection_is_not_the_check: The runner passes a redaction flag, so a captured value never reached the artifact in the first place. That is upstream protection in a runner this run may not edit, and it is not a substitute for the assertion above, which is made against this file's own bytes.

prohibitions_observed.no_coercion_recorded_as_expected_behavio: The single most important prohibition for this file. No row here carries a start_line derived from a string, from an EndLine, from a column or from a fingerprint, and the rejected record carries no start_line at all. An expected file that recorded a coerced value would license the coercion permanently, since the adapter would then be asserted to agree with it.
prohibitions_observed.no_cross_tool_interpretation: Trivy's adapter also reports secrets, and three other adapters can produce this same rejection class. A location or a condition both tools reach is two rows or two rejections in two expected files with no comment: nothing here compares tools, ranks them, explains why one found something another did not, or folds one into the other (AAP 0.3.2). The sibling non-integer fixtures are cited for coverage bookkeeping only -- which value each carries -- never to contrast the tools.
prohibitions_observed.no_judging: No row is characterised as real, important, a false positive or a duplicate, and no row's rule or location is glossed as the sort of thing that tends to be one. The rejected record is not judged either: it is counted for a structural reason -- its start_line is a string -- and nothing here says whether what it reported was worth reporting.
prohibitions_observed.no_dedup: Three elements share a RuleID and a Description and all three become rows. Three records, three rows, and no collapsing of any of them into the others.
prohibitions_observed.no_invented_severity: The tool defines no severity vocabulary, so none is invented: severity_native stays null and severity_norm comes from the fixed no-vocabulary policy rather than from a guess at what a finding deserves. The rejected record gets no severity at all, not even a default.
prohibitions_observed.kept_not_filtered: The out-of-glob lockfile row is kept with in_scope false and counted, never dropped (AAP 0.9.3). Only evidence about the runner establishes a wrong scan root (AAP 0.8.3), and the recorded metadata shows this runner resolved the pinned root.
prohibitions_observed.rejected_not_dropped: The defective record is counted under a named class with its sub-reason retained, not silently discarded. A dropped record would leave rows plus rejections short of the independent record count, which is the arithmetic that makes silent dropping detectable.
prohibitions_observed.never_derived_by_running_the_adapter: Every value in this file was read out of the fixture and the authored contracts -- the fixture's six elements, adapters/gitleaks.py's five-step classification order, its _start_line branches, its _safe_value_repr rendering and its counter set, paths.py's rejection vocabulary and path kinds, emit.py's field order and absence convention, severity.py's no-vocabulary result, reconcile.py's count unit and cli.py's parse-status vocabulary. Nothing here was produced by invoking the adapter and recording its output, which would make the test a tautology: the adapter would be asserted to agree with itself.
prohibitions_observed.agreement_check_disclosed: After these values were derived and written, the adapter was invoked over this fixture once with the real metadata, root and allowlist, and its rows, rejections, detail, record identity and counters compared to what is recorded here; agreement was complete. That check followed derivation, could only ever have surfaced a disagreement to diagnose, and contributed no value to this file. A reader who wants the derivation checked should check it against the fixture and the contracts, which is what every row_derivations entry below is for.

corroboration.agreement: complete once the derivation is accounted for
corroboration.note: All five surviving rows have counterparts in the positive sibling: this file's rows[0] is that file's row 0, rows[1] its row 1, rows[2] its row 2, rows[3] its row 3 and rows[4] its row 5. Of the sixty field comparisons, fifty-eight are identical -- including every null and both in_scope values -- and the two differences are both start_line: its row 2 carries 167 where this file carries null, and its row 3 carries 46 where this file carries null. Those are exactly the two values this fixture's derivation removed, so the disagreement is the derivation being visible rather than a discrepancy. Recorded after the fact rather than as the source of these values: each was derived from the fixture and the authored contracts, so a future disagreement between this file and the adapter is a finding to diagnose rather than a diff to apply.
corroboration.defective_element_has_no_counterpart: The rejected record has nothing to corroborate against and needs nothing: its element appears in no other fixture, it contributes no dataset row, and its expected outcome is checkable by reading the fixture and _start_line. Its captured ancestor's row in the positive sibling is cited under boundary_case for the file's sound line only, not as a counterpart for this record.

rejections.locator_note: The pointer and the array index name the same element, and the array index is also what the produced Rejection carries: adapters/gitleaks.py builds this rejection through paths.make_rejection at step 5 and passes record_index and rule_id, so a produced record_identity and the expectation below can be compared directly without translating one coordinate system into the other.
rejections.reject_class_authority: harness/lib/normalize/paths.py, the REJECT_NON_INTEGER_START_LINE constant -- a literal member of paths.REJECT_CLASSES, the closed set of ten. Written verbatim rather than paraphrased, and to be asserted against the module rather than by eye: a test that only counts rejections cannot tell one condition from another, so the class name is what carries the assertion.
rejections.reject_class_description: a start_line is present but is not an integer
rejections.reject_class_is_produced_by_this_adapter: Yes, and by its own check rather than by a resolver: gitleaks.REJECT_CLASSES_PRODUCED lists this class among the six, and the first four of those six are raised by the adapter's own steps. So unlike the path classes there is no divergence between the fixture's name and the class it exercises.
rejections.classification_step: step 5 of the adapter's fixed classification order -- shape, rule identifier, message, path, start_line. Steps 1 to 4 all pass on this record: it is a JSON object, it carries a non-empty string RuleID, it carries a non-empty string Description, and its File resolves cleanly. That is deliberate, so the only thing left to reject it for is the type of its start_line.
rejections.path_resolution_note: Its File is a root-relative path to a real file in the tree, so the path step succeeds and the record reaches step 5. The resolved path appears in no field of this file: a record that produced no row contributes no field to the dataset, and recording its path here would invite a reader to treat it as a row that was merely mislabelled. The file is named in prose under boundary_case, which is a statement about the fixture rather than a value asserted for the record.
rejections.multi_location_check_ran: The adapter takes the multi-location count before the path step, so this record was inspected for a second location and found to name none -- SymlinkFile is the empty string. Worth stating because it is the one counter a rejected record can still move.
rejections.no_coercion: The expected outcome is a rejection, not a row with start_line 5 and not a row with start_line "5". Nothing in this pipeline converts the string: emit.py refuses a non-integer in that field, and the adapter never offers it one. The value is quoted here as evidence of what the artifact contained, and quoting it is not carrying it.
rejections.adjacent_values_deliberately_unread: The same record carries EndLine 5, StartColumn 1 and EndColumn 1, all integers, and an EndLine equal in value to the string in StartLine is the most tempting inference this fixture offers. None of them is read. Deriving the start from the end, or from a column, would be exactly the inference AAP 0.5.4 forbids -- and here it would produce a row that looked correct and was even at a real line of the file, which is precisely why the temptation is worth naming.
rejections.range_is_not_the_fault: 5 is that file's real last line, so this record is not out of range and no range-based expectation is recorded for it. The class it lands under is decided by the type before any range question is asked, and the below-one route of the same class is not exercised by this fixture at all -- see start_line_policy.below_one_hazard.
rejections.expected_detail: StartLine is a str rather than an integer
rejections.expected_detail_note: The detail is the sub-reason AAP 0.5.4 requires a rejection to carry, and it is quoted in full because this class covers three routes -- a non-integer type, a boolean, and an integer below one. Naming the class alone would not distinguish this record from a StartLine of true or of 0. The adapter composes it as the key's name, then _safe_value_repr of the raw value, then fixed prose; because the raw value is a str, _safe_value_repr names its type rather than rendering it, which is why the detail says 'a str' and contains no value from the record. A test may assert it exactly or by its distinguishing substrings. The same class is fixed for the SARIF adapter in expected/reject-sarif-non-integer-start-line.rows.json, whose expected detail renders the offending value instead of naming its type, because adapters/sarif.py composes it differently. One class, two detail forms -- which is a second reason a test asserting the class alone is not enough in either file, and the reason this file's detail must not be copied from that one.
rejections.record_identity_note: Two keys, and only two. The adapter builds this rejection itself and supplies record_index and rule_id; the RuleID, StartLine, File and reported_path keys that appear on a path rejection are added by the resolver, and the resolver did not reject this record. Enough to find the element in the artifact again, and never the record itself and never a captured value. Note in particular that the identity does not carry the offending value: the detail names its type and the identity names the record, so neither channel carries it.
rejections.why_not_a_row: There are two wrong rows available and no right one. A row with start_line 5 would assert the artifact stated an integer it did not state -- and would be indistinguishable from a sound row, since 5 is a real line of that file. A row with start_line null would assert the artifact stated nothing, which is the opposite of what it did and is indistinguishable from the two legitimate absences in this same fixture. Counting it under a named class keeps the record visible and keeps the arithmetic honest.
rejections.contributes_no_counter: Neither a path_kind_* counter, nor a severity_basis_* counter, nor severity_absent, nor either in_scope counter moves for this record, even though its path resolved: all of them are incremented after step 5. It did pass through the multi-location check, which is taken earlier and found nothing. That asymmetry is the classification order made visible, not a miscount.
rejections.contributes_no_severity_literal: The rejected record is never fed to the severity tally, so no entry from it reaches severity-map.md. That document reports against the rows the dataset contains, and this record contributes none -- which is why severity_absent is 5 rather than 6.
rejections.has_no_in_scope_value: in_scope is a property of a resolved path on an emitted row. This record has no row, so it is neither in scope nor out of scope -- it is counted. A file that recorded in_scope false for it would be asserting that the allowlist had been consulted about a row that was never produced.
rejections.not_produced_by_any_other_condition: The four sibling reject-gitleaks-* fixtures own the other conditions this adapter can produce -- malformed_record, missing_rule_id, missing_message and the path classes -- and this record meets none of them: it is an object, its RuleID and Description are non-empty strings, and its File resolves. So this fixture re-covers nothing they cover, and each of them still has its own work to do.

in_scope_verification.method: Each of the five surviving paths was matched against the twelve globs by hand and then checked twice more, with two implementations that are not the one under test: a glob-to-regex translation written for this check, and CPython 3.13's PurePosixPath.full_match, whose ** spans zero or more directories. All three agree on all five paths, and on which glob each matched.
in_scope_verification.why_not_fnmatch: Three of the twelve globs depend on ** matching zero or more directories, and neither fnmatch nor PurePath.match provides those semantics. A matcher built on either silently drops whole modules, and a silently dropped module looks exactly like a module with nothing to report (AAP 0.5.4).
in_scope_verification.src_test_rule: The exclusion is the literal substring src/test, and it overrides a positive glob match. No path here contains it, including the Python test module, whose test-ness is expressed as a tests/ directory and a test_ filename rather than a Maven src/test tree.
in_scope_verification.the_rejected_record_is_not_in_this_check: in_scope is a property of a resolved path on an emitted row, and the rejected record produced none, so it was not matched against the allowlist at all. Its path would have matched core/src/main/** had it become a row, and that counterfactual is deliberately recorded nowhere in the rows or counters.
in_scope_verification.result: four in scope, one out of scope and kept, one record counted rather than scoped
